utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is the case IT-03-69-T, The Prosecutor versus Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. I would like to move, only for a very short moment, into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Before I give an opportunity to the Prosecution to call its next witness, I'd like to read an oral decision on a request for protective measures for Witness B-1459. The Chamber will now deliver an oral decision on the remainder of the Prosecution's motion for protective measures for witnesses filed on the 6th of January, 2010, and on the remainder of the Prosecution request for leave to reply to the Stanisic Defence response to the Prosecution motion for protective measures for witnesses filed on the 21st of January, 2010, in as far as they relate to Witness B-1459. The Chamber recalls that, on the 25th of January, 2010, it ruled on these motions in as far as they concerned Witness B-1048. In its 6th of January motion, the Prosecution requests that Witness B-1459 be granted a pseudonym and face distortion. The Prosecution states that this witness is a survivor of a so-called human shield incident who was originally scheduled to testify as a Prosecution witness about the same incident in a domestic case before the Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina, to which I will now refer to as the BiH Court. Witness B-1459 reported that, in 2008, he received two telephone calls from an unidentified caller who warned him, inter alia, to be extremely careful. Witness B-1459 also reported that he believes that these phone calls were related to his expected testimony before the BiH Court. The Stanisic Defence, in its response of the 20th of January, 2010, argues that Witness B-1459's fears are subjective that they were expressed only after being solicited by the Prosecution. In relation to the two telephone calls, the Stanisic Defence contends that there is little evidence that the calls were related to the witness's intended testimony in the BiH Court and even less that they could be related to his testimony in the present case. The Simatovic Defence did not respond to the motion. In the 21st of January request to reply, the Prosecution states that it seeks to address certain alleged inaccuracies and incorrect assumptions made by the Stanisic Defence. The Chamber recalls that the party seeking protective measures for a witness must demonstrate an objectively grounded risk to the security or welfare of the witness or the witness's family, should it become known that the witness has given evidence before the Tribunal. This standard may be satisfied by showing that a threat was made against the witness or the witness's family. In examining the request for protective measures, the Chamber has therefore given particular consideration to the threats received by Witness B-1459, as reported by him. The Chamber notes that these threats are of a potentially serious nature and considers that there is a considerable risk that they may have been connected to Witness B-1459's anticipated testimony before the BiH Court. The Chamber further notes that Witness B-1459 is scheduled to testify in the present proceedings about the same incident. Pursuant to Article 20(1) of the Tribunal's Statute and Rule 75 of the Tribunal's Rules of Procedure and Evidence, out of an abundance of caution and considering that the requested protective measures would not affect the public character of the trial, the Chamber therefore grants the protective measures requested by the Prosecution and orders that Witness B-1459 shall be referred to by his pseudonym in all public proceedings and filings and that he shall testify with the protective measures of face distortion - where I said measures, of course, I meant the protective measure of face distortion. Furthermore, in light of this decision, the Chamber denies the remainder of the Prosecution's request for leave to reply, in as far as it concerns Witness B-1459. And this concludes the Chamber's decision. Is the Prosecution ready to call its next witness? No protective measures.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Only one matter which I'd like already to draw your attention to is that part of the 92 ter statements are -- were given in private session. If I say 92 ter statements, I should have said 92 ter testimony. And I do not know what consequences you will attach to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Just a moment, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honours, perhaps private session for one moment to answer the question fully, if you will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you give evidence in this Court, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration, the text of which is now handed out to you by the Usher. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated, Mr. Lazarevic. You gave your solemn declaration in English. Do you prefer to give your testimony in English as well, Mr. Lazarevic, because we --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have interpreters here who could translate your words if you would prefer to speak your own language, your native language.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Actually, I would rather speak in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You'd rather speak in English. Mr. Lazarevic, you will first be examined by Ms. Marcus. Ms. Marcus is counsel for the Prosecution. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Could you kindly state your full name, date, and place of birth for the record.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Slobodan Lazarevic, 26th of February, 1947, Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Can you please tell the Court where and when -- sorry. Where and what it was that you studied?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Languages at university of philosophy.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Do you recall giving evidence before this Tribunal in the case against Slobodan Milosevic on 29th through 31st of October of the year 2002?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And have you --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you make pauses, breaks between questions and answers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, from reading the transcripts in the Milosevic case, it's not the first time that you are reminded to -- not to go into -- too high a speed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My brain goes too fast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Take your time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. I will.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, have you had the opportunity to review the evidence that you gave during that testimony before coming to court today in a language which you understand?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now that you have taken the solemn declaration, do you affirm the truth and accuracy of your prior evidence?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: If I were to ask you the same questions today which you were asked then, would you provide the very same answers?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honours the Prosecution tenders Mr. Lazarevic's testimony in the Slobodan Milosevic case, dated the 29th through the 31st of October, 2002, into evidence under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Madam Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P224, under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P224 is admitted into evidence, under seal. I hereby inform the public that this evidence is admitted under seal because there are smaller portions of the evidence given in private session. However, the remainder of the evidence is accessible through the Internet web site of the ICTY, cases, Slobodan Milosevic case. If you are looking for the transcript, you'll find them sorted by date, and it is the transcript of the 29th, the 30th, and the 31st of October, 2001 [sic]. This is for purposes of the public character of this trial. I said 2001 and I meant to say 2002. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The Prosecution would also like to tender the associated exhibits to that prior testimony. We have, as has become our custom, prepared a list of the prior -- the associated exhibits. We can distribute hard copies to those present if that would be of assistance. For your information and for the record, there are no 65 ter exhibits which have already been admitted, so there is no green row on this. And with Your Honours' leave, I would be happy to submit this around. We're tendering, with your leave, the associated exhibits to the prior testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are there any objections against admission, because we have the -- I would say the administrative matter that numbers should be assigned to them, but I'd first like to know whether there are any objections against admission into evidence of the associated exhibits. We'll any way invite Madam Registrar to assign numbers to them. No decision will be taken until this has been done. So, therefore, the parties -- of course, were aware of the associated exhibits still have an opportunity to express themselves on it. Then, meanwhile, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, in your prior evidence in the Milosevic case, you explained that you served in the Serbian military intelligence unit. Can you describe briefly for the Chamber the structure of the Serbian Military Intelligence Service, KOS?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very briefly, there are two strains within the KOS, and one is to deal with internal security of the country, another one is to deal with the external security of the country. My role was in external security of the country.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Could you tell the Chamber the years of your service in KOS.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Basically from 1968 to 1998.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And who was your direct handler?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Colonel Nicola Zimonja.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, when were you first deployed to the region of the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: In 1991, very early 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Who was it who originally placed you there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, I attended a meeting late 1991, between Toso Pajic, Djuro Skaljac, and Colonel Zimonja. And it was suggested that I should transfer to Samarice which then was a command post for the 8th Operational Group under the command of General Mrksic, and that's -- I went there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Where precisely were you deployed then within the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Originally it was the HQ of the JNA in Samarice which is also known as the 8th Operative Group. And upon the formation of the corps, I was transferred to the area of the 21st Corps or, as it is also known, Kordun Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now just for clarification, when I asked you when you were first deployed to the Krajina, your answer was in very early 1991. And then when I asked you who placed you there, you described a meeting in late 1991 where it was decided that you would be transferred. Could you possibly clarify the dates for us?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: It's a mistake, obviously a mistake that I just made. I arrived to the Krajina region late 1991. I would say probably around 22nd or 23rd of December. And within a week to ten days, I was transferred to Samarice which is in the vicinity of Glina. So that would be the beginning of 1992. I'm sorry. I'm just getting too old.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now what was your sector called, the sector where you were deployed?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: It was named according to the UN as Sector North, but in our own naming of the sectors it was actually the sector which is AOR of the 21st Corps. And that falls between the two corps and my right-hand side would be Banja Corps, 39 Corps; and on my left would be Lika Corps, or the 19th Corps. So all those three --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness slow down, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. All those three corps areas were under the Sector North deployment.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Officially --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, if you say to your right or to your left, for us to understand --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I'm facing Zagreb as I'm facing you, then the Banja Corps would be on my right and the Lika Corps on my left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Lika to the west, the other one to the east?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Officially, within the Krajina, what was your job, officially?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I was liaison officer for the 21st Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Can you define for us the role of the liaison officer. What did it mean to be the liaison officer?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Basically organising the meetings between the command of the Sector North of the UN and the HQ of the 21st Corps, and dealing with all the other international bodies that would come up, like International Red Cross or ECMM or even journalists. It would go through me.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Officially, within the Krajina, to whom did you report?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I had two -- two lines of reporting. One was to my CO, Colonel Cedo Bulat, who was a commanding officer of the 21st --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness slow down when he gives names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm fighting for a breath that's why I'm trying to squeeze too much in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you take a breath first and then continue speaking, then that might assist the others.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. My apologies again. [Overlapping speakers] ... back there were two lines of reporting as far as I was concerned: One as a liaison officer, 21st Corps, I would report directly to Colonel Cedo Bulat. The other line was the reporting -- virtually on a daily basis to my KOS line which was Colonel Nikola Zimonja. In between, I also had a few times to report other requests of the KOS to report to the local police.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: From whom did you receive your salary?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Again, from two different sources. As an officer of the 21st Corps of the Army of the Republika Srpska Krajina, I would receive my monthly salary from Knin. But some other benefits I would receive from -- from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, can you tell us how were the corps of the army of the Republika Srpska Krajina, the ARSK, how were the corps formed?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I can really only try to explain how it happened in the Sector North. I don't know what happened in Sector East or Sector South. But in my own AOR, it was very simple. The corps were given names in accordance with the position they held on the ground. So if the Banja had their positions there, it would be a Banja Corps. The 21st Corps would cover the area of -- from Glina to Slunj and that was called Kordun Corps or 21st Corps and would directly join the 19th Corps further south.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: In which -- now just to repeat and clarify, your corps, again, was -- tell us what the name of your corps was?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: 21st Corps. Also known as Kordun Corps. It was covering the area of Kordun.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in your prior evidence, you discuss the demobilisation of the Army of the Serb Republic of Krajina, the demobilisation of the ARSK, pursuant to the Vance Plan. I'd like you to tell us, and please tell us slowly, prior to this demobilisation, from whom did the corps of the ARSK take their directives?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: From the general HQ of JNA which was still then JNA, turns into VJ later on. So instructions and operational movement and everything else would come straight from Belgrade. After the point of us being disarmed in accordance with the Vance Plan, and that meant that there was no more uniformed or military dressed personnel on the ground, over night, we all transformed into police force. Not only the uniforms but also the transportation were over night coloured in blue, which the militia or police colours, instead of being the olive-green, as the military.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Okay. We're going return to that topic in just a moment. But, first, can you tell us, while the corps of the ARSK were being set up, what was taking place with respect to the political structures in the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: One has to take into consideration the situation on the ground. Everything was happening very fast. Even your smallest police station, for example, would have a diminished number of police officers because all those of Croatian origin had left the area. The same applies to all political structures. If you had a mayor and the mayor was a Croatian, he was no longer there so it was needed to elect another mayor for municipalities. So all this was happening within a short space of time of approximately three month, electing the officials, placing them into positions, setting up the numbers with the police, things like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, you've told us that were the liaison officer for the 21st or the Kordun Corps. What area of responsibility did the 21st or Kordun Corps cover precisely from where to where, and what the territory that was covered?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: The length of the territory which was considered to be area the of 21st Corps would be approximately 70 kilometres long, between 17 to 20 kilometres wide. And it was going from Glina to the right or to the east, all the way to Slunj to the left, or to the west.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: In your evidence in the Milosevic case, on the 29th of October, 2002, at transcript page 12319, you explained that the original HQ of the 21st Corps was in Topusko, opposite the UN compound, and that from there the HQ moved to Petrova Gora and from Petrova Gora you moved -- the headquarters moved in early 1993. Can you explain to us what prompted the move of the headquarters of the 21st Corps in early 1993 to Petrova Gora?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, we have found ourselves to be in very close proximity of the HQ of the Sector North, the UN forces. As the crow flies, less than 150 metres away. So the general idea was, This is great; we can actually observe what they do. Then we realise, at the same time, they are observing what we do. So we decided we are going to remove this place, the HQ, to Petrova Gora, with me being left behind in a hotel in Topusko as an officer of the liaison office.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And then what was it that prompted the move later from Petrova Gora to Vojnic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: That was an order issued to us simple to move from Petrova Gora to -- in the vicinity of Vojnic there was, I don't know, a villa there, and I believe that belonged to Minister Spegelj of Croatia. We were taking that position because apparently the special police force from Serbia was moving with that HQ into Petrova Gora. From that day on, it was off limits to us, the members -- or most of the members of the 21st Corps. They had secured the parameter. You could go there only by invitation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Could the Court Officer please call up 65 ter 14. This is a map that was marked by the witness during his testimony in the Milosevic case. And I think it would be helpful if the Court Usher wouldn't mind giving this to the witness and putting it on the ELMO. Perhaps, with a pen, the witness can indicate to us what he is talking about as he describes it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think you're invited -- could you put the map on the ELMO, please. This is a copy which you do not want the markings to be tendered -- the marked version to be tendered into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: The marked version, this very document, with the markings on it, is an associated exhibit, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But you do not want any further markings --

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I don't foresee the need for that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then could this be put on the ELMO so the witness, without further marking the document could, nevertheless, with a pen could explain to us what is he talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The ELMO is not functioning. Therefore, I suggest that whatever the witness wants to explain to us he would do that by marking on the screen, although the markings then not to be further tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: No, problem, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, do you see the map in front of you which you marked during your Milosevic testimony?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Could you please kindly identify to us what is shown on this map, what were the locations that you marked.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: There are several locations on this map that I have marked. So let me start with the well, Petrova Gora is right in the middle. Then you have the line going to the MUP Serbia HQ. Right there. Little red dot now.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, you could circle it just so that we know what you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, what the witness is talking about is what he is reading. It seems to be ... If he says MUP Serbia headquarters, I take it that he is referring to what we find on the screen as the MUP Serbia headquarters and nothing else. I mean ...

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- that is clear for everyone who looks at it. There is, I see, a reference to the 21st Corps' headquarter. And to the original 21st Corps; perhaps that is headquarters as well. We could ask him because that is it not clear from the text itself yet.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I can be of any help. I am pointing at the area of Topusko now. That's where the original HQ of the 21st Corps was situated and the command of the Sector North of the UN. From this position, we moved to Petrova Gora, and then we got displaced by the police from Serbia from Petrova Gora to Vojnic, just above on the map. All the other points here, and that is Pauk HQ -- headquarters, and then RSK parade ground in 1995. That's about it that this map shows.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lazarevic. It was precisely that progressive move and to orient the Court that I wanted to -- to show the map that you had previously marked.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, we can -- now we can leave the map. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: In the Milosevic case, you mentioned -- and just earlier today you also mentioned Colonel Bulat. Can you tell us who he was, with respect to the 21st Corps?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Colonel Bulat is a career officer with the JNA. When I met him, he a rank of Colonel and he was Chief of Staff to General Mrksic in Samarice, 8th Operational Group, HQ. Upon the formation of the corps, he was promoted to a corps commander of the 21st Corps in Kordun area.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: In your prior evidence you describe a so-called anti-terrorist unit of the Kordun Corps. Can you tell us, was this anti-terrorist unit present within the corps throughout the time-period that you were there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were from 1992 -- from 1992 to the fall of 1995. When I say fall, I meant the fall of RSK.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: In the Milosevic case, on the 29th of October of 2002, on page 12323, you said that this anti-terrorist unit carried out "dirty jobs." You then said of this group: "They are used to scare people. They are used to create disturbances." Why would there have been tasks to scare people or create disturbances?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: There are a number of reasons for it. If the things were not tense enough in the area, it will affect the black market, the prices will go down. So they would create disturbance anywhere along the frontier of the 21st Corps to Croatia and automatically it will close down all the roads leading to these points of sale, if you like. And the prices will go up within ten days. That was the reason on the ground. But there were other reasons as well. One was a purely political reason. Because every time the situation would go little bit, let's call it reasonable, Belgrade didn't like that, because immediately the international organisations would start suggesting that we should start negotiating with Croatia the situation on the ground. Now, I don't think that Belgrade liked the idea of any negotiation. So that would also now create the situation with a -- well, we cannot really negotiate because cease-fire agreement was broken here, and was broken there. Things like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: To your knowledge, who provided the funding for the anti-terrorist unit of the 21st Corps? Were they on the payroll of the 21st Corps?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: They were not on the payroll of the 21st Corps, but -- according to themselves, Because I knew, I would say, 90 per cent of those boys. There were all young men in their early 20s. The only thing in common that they had was an extensive police record at that young age. And they claimed they got paid by the police, Serbia. They claim, again. But they did not pay through our -- they did not get paid through our pay master of the 21st Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, prior to the demobilisation under the Vance Plan, can you describe the relationship between the military forces and the police forces on the ground in the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: In my former country of Yugoslavia there was always antagonism between the police and the military. Two of the biggest soccer clubs in Belgrade, Partizan and Red Star, one was run by a police, Red Star, and Partizan by army. And that's just to show you what the really relationship between two was. There was always kind of a competition; who was going to come up front as bigger and better than the previous one. Now, in RSK at the time, early 1992, admittedly the army had the upper hand, simply because of the situation that developed or did not development at the time gave more importance to the army. But they were the one to defend the population in -- in Krajina. So the police kind of took a second stand, if you like.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: On page 12330, when you were asked how the Vance Plan affected the army of the RSK, you said: "The Vance Plan required total demilitarisation and demobile of all units within the RSK. Us being co-signatories of the plan, what we did, we changed the uniform overnight from military olive-green into the police blue and within a very short period of time, I'd say within ten hours, we have repainted all the military vehicles into the blue colour, being -- representing the police." Did this change affect you directly, and if so, how?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, the only difference that I kind of felt directly, I guess, is I was issued the police ID, I was transformed into a police officer or still within the same area I had the same duties, the officers were still the same, some of them were in police uniforms and some were in civilian. I would attend all the meetings in the Sector North command of the UN dressed as a civilian, really. For the time being.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: On that same page, 12330, you were asked further about the relationship between the army and the police in the RSK, and you said: "Well, at the very beginning, the army had the upper hand in everything that was happening. When I'm talking about the beginning, I'm talking about 1992. Later on, with the presence of the special forces from Serbia, that power has gone into the hands of police." Can you be more specific about what you meant when you said "with the presence of the special forces from Serbia, that power had gone into the hands of the police"?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: From the very beginning of creating the RSK, most of the conscripts came from the population within the RSK. So the army had advantage of selecting the best for them, not the police. So the police, really, at the beginning, was very shorthanded. They couldn't do virtually apart from this daily routine jobs like patrols or investigation, likes that. After demobilisation, suddenly we are now all in the police. Now the police could actually keep those who were educated, who were trained, keep them in their own ranks. After we had mobilisation again, they never returned them to us. They stayed with the police.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Can you explain a bit more about what you were referring to here when you said the special forces from Serbia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: There so many names attributed to this unit that came across that -- well, I'm using "special force." Maybe they used another name; I don't know. But the point of the fact is we had a sudden influx of uniformed personnel within the area of the 21st Corps. They had different uniforms, different shoulder insignias, different badges on their soldiers. And if you managed to speak to any one of them, you'd realise very clearly that they are coming from Serbia, by the accent they use. And as I said, it was a sudden influx, at least myself, personally, I was not prepared for that. And I remember being asked by the military observers of the UN and the sector commander of the UN, Who are these people suddenly on ground? And my instruction was to tell the UN general on the ground, Well, they are really only passing through. I had no idea they were going to stop or be involved in anything until we were asked to leave the Petrova Gora HQ and give it to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: How did the increased presence of the special forces from Serbia affect operations of the 21st Corps?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Affected it in many ways, really. I think, suddenly, we find ourselves to have a secondary importance in the area of the 21st Corps. There were areas of the 21st Corps that we were not allowed to go into anymore. There were parts of the 21st Corps that the military observers wanted to go; we had to prevent them from going there. I think that the special force from police just didn't want to be known that they are there for the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I just waited for the witness to finish. I would like to ask my colleague and also the Chamber and that would be easier for us to prepare for the cross-examination if we could be told the time-period that this witness is referring to. We're talking about all of this, but we don't know to which time-period this refers. It will be easier for us for the cross-examination, because our time is also limited for -- to be able to explore exactly the time-period he is thinking of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apparently in relation to the last answer, could you tell us when this was that you were instructed to tell that they were just passing by and when they came to the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Beginning of 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Beginning of 1993. Please proceed, Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, was this when the 21st Corps HQ moved from Petrova Gora to Vojnic, as you said before?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Who was ultimately responsible for events on the ground at this stage, so after the Vance Plan's demobilisation?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't quite understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Let me repeat. Who was ultimately, to your knowledge, responsible for events on the ground after the demobilisation?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, apparently it was supposed to be the Army of Republika Srpska Krajina. But basically all the supplies, the ammunition, and fuel, everything came from Belgrade. So I can suggest that their needs were supplied in a written form to the HQ of the JNA to Belgrade, and they would forward to us. So if you want the ultimate responsibility, was the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And again, for time-period, are you talking about before the demobilisation or after the demobilisation?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Before and very, very brief time after. It was taken over by police. Because suddenly there was actually a police force on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to ask the Court Officer to call up 65 ter 653 which is a chart that was used by the witness, prepared by the witness, to explain the relationships of different organs in the Krajina. Perhaps the B/C/S version might be put on one side for ease of reference for those who don't speak English.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, can you tell us what time-period does this command structure which you prepared, what time-period does it cover?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I made -- I made this map in 1999. But this would cover anything from early 1992 to the -- May 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honours, due to the horizontal nature of the chart, I can either suggest, as Your Honours wish, that we call it up only in English on the screen, full screen; or, again, that we try to use the ELMO for the witness to point. I don't -- again I don't envisage any marking necessary, but I'm at your disposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I suggest that we use the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court, please, what this chart represents?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Basically it represents the power structure of what was happening in RSK in Sector North that I know of. If you look at it very carefully you can see the squares. And the whole squares within the scares, they're all interconnected. So really they're working as one body. You have your army structure to your right on the screen, going all the way down to the anti-terrorist unit. Then have you a line that goes straight to General Momcilo Perisic at the General HQ. And they leaned to Pauk formation of the commander Pauk right there in the middle. And to the left you have Arkan forces. You have SDB of Serbia there with Mr. Stanisic on top, and Simatovic below, and Colonel Bozovic. Then you have a little corner there with Toso Pajic who was the chief of police who became minister of internal affairs in the RSK. Next name, you have a representative of the DB of Serbia, Milos Pajic, who was originally there before the conflict. Then you have some RSK politicians which are mostly in the eye of the public at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: We're going to elaborate a little bit on some of these relationships as we move forward. I'm going to ask you -- I'm going to refer, again, to some of your prior testimony and ask you to clarify or further explain some of the things you said in -- in connection with these relationships. When you were asked at page 12362 about the box marked SDB Serbia, you were asked to describe the relationships depicted in that part of the diagram. And your response was: "At the head of the SDB Serbia at the time was Mr. Stanisic, Jovica. His direct assistants were Frenki, also known as Simatovic or Stamatovic, followed by Colonel Ulemek, Legija, and Colonel Bozovic. And then within the circle you also see Mr. Toso Pajic was the chief of police and liaison officer of the RSK, and his direct line goes to the SDB Serbia, Mr. Stanisic, and RSK MUP minister of the Internal Affairs, also Milos Pajic, head of state security. And all connected directly to Jovica Stanisic." Can you elaborate specifically on what you meant when you said that that "all connected directly to Jovica Stanisic"?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: All and any police structure on the ground was ultimately responsible to Mr. Stanisic, including the Pauk commanders which consisted from three different sources. I mean, if you look at it, Major-General Mile Novakovic at the head of the Pauk, and yet he was an officer of the RSK. And you had Fikret Abidc who was leading his own western Bosnia forces. And with them, you go the line through Arkan Colonel Pejovic, Colonel Sarac, all the way to Colonel Bozovic, Colonel Ulemek, and "Gospodine" Simatovic and "Gospodine" Stanisic. So they are really all kind of a package deal.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: How did you know this to be the case?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, I was there. I was present on the ground when these things were happening.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Who was the head of the state security division within the RSK?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: In my sector was Mr. Milos Pajic, at least he introduced himself as one.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, you also described Toso Pajic whose name we see on this chart as well. What was his role as compared with the role of Milos Pajic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: In real terms, I believe that Toso Pajic had more influence than Milos ever had. Toso Pajic was to become a minister of interiors for the RSK, but he was in a -- he was in constant connection with all these people SDB Serbia which led me to believe that actually he worked for SDB Serbia before. And I only got a confirmation when we all moved to Belgrade to find out he already had an office waiting for me within the SDB building. And he had another office within the building which was considered to be a government in exile were to retain his position as minister of internal affairs.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Can you describe what relationship you had with Toso Pajic, if any?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: My relationship with Mr. Pajic as extremely cordial and I liked the man, really, as a person. He was well educated. I believe he was studying in France at one time. He spoke French fluently which helped us to deal with the French Battalion in the Velika Kladusa area. And I found him to be a perfect gentleman, so. And we spent a lot of time together.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: On pages 12336 and 12337, you were asked whether, during your daily contacts with Toso Pajic, he told you who he works for. You stated: "On numerous occasions, he stated that he actually works for Jovica Stanisic who was head of the state security in Serbia proper." Can you elaborate further on your knowledge of Toso Pajic's relationship to Jovica Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: As I have stated before, I had at least five times a week meetings with Mr. Pajic, because simply we were coordinating our work between the military and the police as far as the UN forces on the ground are concerned. So quite frequently I would be in his office and he would tell me, like, you know, Daddy's on the ground; daddy's coming tomorrow; he will be here. And I was led to believe that Daddy is Mr. Stanisic. And he had always this little smile on his face when he was talking about Stanisic. He never -- actually, I have to be honest about it, he never directly said, I am working for Stanisic. But he did do all the work. It has been proven that actually he did work for Stanisic in the end.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: What do you mean when you say "it has been proven that he actually did work for Stanisic in the end"?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: He was relocated to Belgrade. He went straight to the DB building and he got his office there. I visited him there. And in his office, within the building, which was taken over by the government of RSK in exile.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: How long did the Serbian DB maintain their presence in the Krajina, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: DB Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Probably through the last three days of existence of the RSK; they pulled out first.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: In your prior evidence and also here today, you've been referring to something called Pauk. Your prior evidence describes a Pauk Joint Command, "Pauk" meaning "spider." In describing the Pauk Command's establishment, you said during your testimony on page 12352: "Special forces were deployed in our area prior to establishment of a new HQ on the Bosnian side in the vicinity of Velika Kladusa, code-named Pauk, meaning spider." Could you clarify what you meant in this case, when you referred to special forces being deployed?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: It does need a bit longer an explanation than a simple sentence or two. At the time in 1993 most of us were distracted to revive our relationship with Fikret Abdic. There were a few of us that were against it, but, then again, the order came from Belgrade so we went along with it. The situation developed that the forces from Serbia, the special police force in Serbia, got into the area of the 21st Corps and formed a Joint Command of a special forces from Serbia military personnel from the 21st Corps, military personnel of Zapadni Bosnia, under Mr. Fikret Abdic. And also the Arkan's Tigers, they were there to. So, the HQ of the Pauk was established approximately 200 yards inside Bosnia. So they are no longer in Croatia; they're inside Bosnia. Then approximately 6-, to 800 metres away was the second command of the Pauk which was held by Mr. Frenki Simatovic. So there was a close coordination between what was happening in Pauk and in Bosnia and Pauk in Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Just for clarification, the second command of the Pauk which was, you say, headed by Mr. Frenki Simatovic, in which territory was that located?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: In Croatia, if that's easier for people to understand. But the RSK was a part of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now you were asked on this very point on page 12356 to describe what, if any, relationship Arkan's group, Arkan's Tigers had with the Army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, and your answer was: "Well, Arkan's" --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, could I object to the leading nature of this question. This evidence is extremely contentious. And to lead the witness to the answer he previously gave, in our submission, is not a fair way to proceed. What my learned friend should do is ask the witness what his evidence is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. As a matter of fact, if Ms. Marcus quotes from his previous evidence, she just goes back to what is already in evidence. Isn't it? That's -- what is on page 12356, I take it that Ms. Marcus wants to give -- to seek follow-up evidence or -- but that's evidence at this moment. The witness has testified that he has reviewed this and that he would give the same answers, and then, when tendered, these transcripts were admitted into evidence. So to say you're leading the witness, you're taking the witness back to what is already in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: If that's the position, then I withdraw the objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: So in answer to that question --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The speakers are kindly asked to slow down for the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: In answer to that question of what relationship Arkan's group, Arkan's Tigers had with the Army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, you stated: "Well, Arkan's forces were deployed in the Pauk HQ and were then put with the MUP of Serbia and the members of the 21st Corps." Can you show us on your command chart where this joint Pauk Command is reflected.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you mean on the map in front of me?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, the command chart in front of you.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Under the heading of Pauk HQ Bosnia, Major-General Milo Novakovic, you have Fikret Abdic. To the left you have Captain Sarac, Colonel Pejovic, which are the officers of the Arkan's Tigers. Arkan himself, personally, maybe, I don't know, maybe went once or twice. He wasn't there throughout, but these people were. And above them you have Colonel Bozovic, Colonel Ulemek, and Frenki Simatovic as members of the DB. So these are the three sides that make the combined HQ.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Can you explain briefly who Fikret Abdic was?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I used to work for the man. I was employed by Agrokomerc before the conflict. And he is the man who had the vision of creating Kladusa to be the food maker of the world. And he did succeed to the one point and something went bad, and he -- you know. But it was an extremely large company employed most of the people from the region there. It was a food producing plant. It was making biscuits and chicken and I don't know what not. It was making everything; chocolates. His idea was - if I can just go back to the elections in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time - when he beat Alija Izetbegovic in elections hands down and then refused to become the first president of the Bosnia, didn't want it, he wanted to go back and deal with Agrokomerc which he considered to be his child. When they had decided to make these arrangements with Fikret Abdic to secure the position of Velika Kladusa and all the plants around it, how they came about it, I don't know. But apparently they did make an agreement. Hence, the people like Simatovic and Ulemek and Bozovic and everybody else that was there moved in to secure the sector which was then called western Bosnia. Basically what you had the case of Muslims fighting the Muslims with aid of special police from Serbia. If you could picture, I don't know if it's possible, really, the 21st Corps didn't really like the idea of having behind them 5th Corps. They would rather have these command forces of Fikret Abdic as some of other fighters there and have their lines secured. So as a military point, from the 21st Corps of getting involved in that. The other one is a pure marketing. Mr. Abdic had warehouses in Rijeka. Now, producing his -- whatever he was producing at the time in Velika Kladusa had to be transported to Rijeka then to be shipped all over the world. But he can only do it going through the AOR of the 21st Corps, because we're in position between Croatia and them. The length of about, as I said before, maybe 17 kilometres. So you had to secure this passageway to Croatia. So the whole deal was, kind of, working for all sides involved.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now on page 12422, when you were asked a bit more about the Pauk Joint Command, and when you became aware of this Joint Command, you stated: "It was late 1993 when there was a sudden influx of these men, uniforms I had never encountered before. Talking to them in our own language it was obvious they're not from the area. Also, it was obvious they're not a paramilitary unit as far as we're concerned, because they were given a free passageway and also they were given our old HQ in Petrova Gora." Can you explain what you meant when you said that talking to them in your own language it was obvious they were not from the area?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: There was one officially language of former Yugoslavia called Serbo-Croatian which kind of split into Serbia and then in Croatia. And you can -- by just listening people speak, you can tell whether they are Croatian or Serbs or which part of Serbia they would come or whether they are from Montenegro. You take a good example of Colonel Bozovic who had a very thick Montenegrin accent; you cannot miss it. If you talk to Colonel Ulemek, he spoke Ekavski. Now people from the area, they all speak Ijkavski. If they're born in Kordun and lived in Kordun or even if they're Croatian were [indiscernible] behind, so you had a Ekavski/Ijkavski/Chakavski/Ikavski [phoen] -- I mean, you know, there is a multitude of all these little dialects that would separate same nation into smaller groups where they come from.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: So which dialect was it that was spoken?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Ekavski in the majority of the cases. If you were talking to the members of the special police, yes, absolutely, Ekavski. Which I speak myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And, just for clarification, Ekavski come from what region?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Serbia. There are probably a multitude of places that also speak Ekavski. I mean, when I say Serbia, I'm talking about the general rule. If you speak Ekavski, you're Serbian from Serbia, end of story. There are some situations around Banja Luka when they wanted now to sound more Serbian then they really are, they are forcing Ekavski in their schools and in public meetings and everything. But it's not natural. They do speak a version of Serbian which is spoken in Bosnia which is Ijkavski?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, what did you mean when you said they were given free passageway?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, simply they could go where I couldn't. As a liaison officer. As I said before, for me to go to Pauk, I need a special pass to go into Bosnia to the Pauk Command, and I had reasons throughout my stay there and in dealing with people that I had to go there. And Colonel Bulat gave me a permanent pass for Pauk. So I couldn't just sit in my car and drive straight into Bosnia and say, Hi, boys, here I am. There were check-points. Before you enter there were check-points there on both sides of the border. And they would check your documents, and they let you go if you had the pass. If you didn't have the pass, you can't go through. You're entering another country and yet nobody asked for passport.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honours, if you would like to take a break, perhaps this is a breaking point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If this would be a suitable moment for you, then we would take the break now. We will resume at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, I'd like to briefly raise a different matter, which is we need a housekeeping session, and the Chamber is considering to have a housekeeping session either on Thursday morning or Thursday afternoon. Now, it is well known that not all accused are always interested in attending housekeeping sessions which is about numbers and about all kind of practicalities. If Mr. Stanisic would want to attend, then the -- we'll not change the rhythm and then we'll schedule it for the afternoon. If, however, Mr. Stanisic would waive his right to be present at such a housekeeping session, then we would consider to have it in the morning. And assuming that it will not take any longer than from 9.00 to 12.00 - and I don't have any reason to believe that - then we could schedule it for the morning. I'd like to hear from the parties at a later moment what their preference is. I see already some body language from Mr. Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I think Your Honour has his opinion. He'd rather not attend. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. He'd rather not attend. Yes. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My colleague Petrovic and I have requested from the Secretariat to be issued a ticket so that we may leave for Serbia on Wednesday in order to conduct some additional investigations. And my request is, if that is not possible, to postpone for this a later date because we have already appointments with some witnesses that we want to meet with in order to rehash some issues, and I don't want to go into all the explanations that you are already familiar with. But we would really appreciate it if you could move this to a later date because we already have all the arrangements made, the tickets prepared, everything arranged with the Registry, and meetings in Serbia with these witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would you please be so kind to -- to communicate with Chamber staff days on which you are -- for days on which it is not possible for you to attend due to these kind of commitments, always for the morning or the afternoon of that day, so that we can further consider the matter. Mr. Groome, I think for the Prosecution it is a bit less of a problem because usually there is one or two members of the team always available here in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I will available, Your Honour, and it's at the convenience of the Chamber and Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we will further consider it, and we'll certainly also keep in mind your commitments, Mr. Bakrac, so ... Then, Ms. Marcus, are you ready to continue?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, I am going to return to the topic that we left off, which was the Pauk Joint Command. I'm going to ask you for some more elaboration and clarifications in relation to some of your prior testimony. You were asked on page 12426 of your prior testimony to give more detail with respect to the numbers and composition of the different forces which made up the Pauk Joint Command. And you replied: "I believe that the members of the 21st Corps were numbered about 400 strong. I would place MUP to about 200, in Arkans to about 100. And I have no knowledge of how many of Abdic's forces were there." When you mentioned MUP, to whom were you referring in this portion of your prior evidence?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: MUP that came from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in relation to the MUP from Serbia, in your prior evidence, on the same page, you stated: "That was actually the special force of police from Serbia proper, headed by Colonel Bozovic, Colonel Ulemek, also known as Legija, apparently he was a former Legionnaire, and Frenki Stamatovic. Frenki Stamatovic held the command in Petrova Gora while the others were across the border in Bosnia." Now, how did you know of the involvement of these individuals in the Pauk Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: By virtue of actually visiting the command and meeting them there, I don't know whether they were aware of me being there, but I had an instance where I had a meeting with Colonel Bozovic in Kladusa itself. That's how I got my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: What can you tell us about the type of weaponry that the Pauk Command had under its control?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: We were actually envious of the MUP from Serbia because they had a superior weapons than we did. Example: Officers that I met carried Heckler & Koch automatic weapons; I don't know if people know or not. A side-weapon was issued to them, Sig Sauer, another very superior gun to ours that we had which were produced in former Yugoslavia and stored it in different places. And then when the conflict started, we were issued with that. So the quality of the uniforms were better than ours. Originally, when I saw them first, I thought the NATO forces are here. That's how good their uniforms looked. And we had uniforms, you know, variety of styles and -- so it was the weapon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the name of the side-arm because I think --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sig Sauer. It's a Swiss-made handgun.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Could I ask the Court Officer to call up 65 ter 406, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, you commented at length on this document during your prior evidence. Could you, here, just briefly for us comment on the significance of this order.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, if you -- if you look at the heading of the letter itself, it says more an order actually than a letter. And it's done by the command of the Pauk. And then in the third line you have all these people that it was addressed to. And then have you a command -- a command of the 21st Corps and 29 Corps. Tactical Group 2; Tactical Group 3; the command of Pauk; and command of the ZB which is a western Bosnia abbreviation, Zapadna Bosna. So you have all these people who are heavily involved in information of Pauk and actively taking part in all the decisions, so whatever is happening on the ground. And then, from 1 to 6, it's listed to send this information back to the Pauk Command, about the number of weapons, the number of ammunition, what the requirements are. So it's that type of document.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And then -- I'm sorry, I was just reading through. Then in the second-last paragraph you have then this should include also the units of MUP. Well, in this case, the MUP is MUP Serbia is not -- not MUP Krajina. And also the units of the RS which is Republika Srpska in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could -- could we move the document so that we can follow the -- and apparently the witness was referring to the portion after number 6. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: So, Mr. Lazarevic, based on your direct knowledge, what do we learn from this order?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, what we learn from this order is actually the -- the number of different units that were involved in Pauk. You got them from Bosnia, you got them from Serbia, you got them from the Krajina, you got them from Bosnia. It's like, I don't know, like an international unit, really. And yet they all worked together. And, by the way, the signature on the bottom, it is Colonel Bulat's signature, because I have seen it so many times.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you. You'll find me just observing a pause. I was reprimanded by our colleagues in the translation booth, so I'm trying to observe a pause between question and answer. Now, when did you first provide the Office of the Prosecutor with information in relation to the Pauk Joint Command; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. In 1999.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: For the record, I would like to note that Mr. Lazarevic gave his first statement to the Office of the Prosecutor in July of 1999.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, on pages 12351 and 12352, you described Toso Pajic showing you a document from Mr. Stanisic regarding cooperation with Fikret Abdic. You explained: "It was a time when, for unknown reason to me, Fikret Abdic and Belgrade have reconciled. And the letter which arrived from Belgrade not only through Stanisic through Toso Pajic also, through the military channels, was to establish a good, neighbourly cooperation with Abdic's forces, which were actually boarding with the 21st Corps area." What do you know about Mr. Stanisic's role with respect to the Joint Pauk Command?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know nothing personally about Mr. Stanisic's involvement apart from -- analysing the situation and seeing that his -- the right-hand man or his number two man in command, Frenki Stanisic, is on the ground. And also from conversation with Toso Pajic and everybody else that Mr. Stanisic does come every now and then but it is not like a 24/7 as Mr. Stanisic is -- I mean, sorry, as Mr. Simatovic is. And I can't really see that Frenki Simatovic has carried all this on his own, without really informing Mr. Stanisic or being directed by Mr. Stanisic in this instance.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: What was your personal position on this issue of cooperation with Abdic's forces?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: My personal condition was, no; adamant no. Because after that point in time in fighting the forces of Fikret Abdic, including the the 5th Corps, Because they were the members of the 5th Corps. So they were the enemies officially. And my knowledge -- some other officers were also against this cooperation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Are you familiar with a man named Colonel Raja Bozovic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think I mentioned him before. He is a Colonel; he is, obviously, of Montenegrin origin because he really, really have this thick Montenegrin accent. And I met him in -- in a huge store in -- where his command was or part of his command in Velika Kladusa when I needed to see him about some exchange of -- of soldiers which have died in combat for exchange. And, might I add, he was very unpleasant. If I can quote him, we were asking for a dead and he said, Well, if you need dead, you go and kill him yourself, find him yourself. But he's not going to offer any.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: In relation to Colonel Bozovic on page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, part of what you say is just lost because you speak too quickly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When you said -- you quoted him that -- if you would ask for bodies that you would say, I'm not going provide them; you have to kill them yourself. That's what I heard from you, but it does not appear on the transcript. If you want your testimony to be reflected on the transcript, I again urge you to slow down. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: On page 12443 of your Milosevic testimony, you were explaining about this exchange of bodies to which it seems you've just referred. And you stated that at one point Colonel Mlado Karan, had asked you to go to the headquarters, and you said: "He directed me to go to Pauk Command and speak to Colonel Bozovic and Colonel Pejovic, one was the MUP Serbia, Bozovic was MUP Serbia, and Pejovic was Arkan's Tigers. See if they can assist." You have just mentioned the circumstances of this meeting. Can you elaborate briefly? What was the circumstance of that meeting to which you're referring?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Through the international mediation, we were offered to exchange the deads with the 5th corps, apparently they claim to have 100 dead Serbian soldiers there and they requested 100 Muslim soldiers for exchange. At that time, the arrangement we had was one for one. So I had a problem finding 100. So I looked all over the place; I went to local police stations -- I don't know. They might have a -- remembering there was one buried here and one buried there; we go and dig them out. Anyway, to make a long story short, we were short people, or short bodies. So when I was discussing this with Colonel Mlado Karan who is in charge of the internal security of the 21st Corps, he suggested I go and see Bozovic and Pejovic, both colonels, since they had been involved in heavy fighting against the 5th Corps, the Bosnian 5th Corps. And that's what I did. And, unfortunately, Colonel Bozovic didn't offer any assistant in that respect. However, Colonel Pejovic did.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Do you know what Colonel Bozovic's reporting line was?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Directly to Mr. Stanisic, or through Frenki.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: You mentioned earlier, briefly, about Arkan. Can you elaborate? Is there anything else you know about Arkan and his role in the Pauk Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me -- you asked, Do you know what Colonel Bozovic's reporting line was. And I understood the answer of the witness to be a request for clarification of that question. Or have I misunderstood you? You said: Directly to Mr. Stanisic or through Frenki. Did you want to have more details as far as the question was concerned, or did you give an answer saying that he was reporting directly to Mr. Stanisic, or, as the case may have been, through Mr. Simatovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Former is correct, meaning he was reporting directly to his superior in command within Pauk, and that was referring to Simatovic. And Frenki Simatovic continued his reporting line to Mr. Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you were not seeking further explanation, but you were answering the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I misunderstood you. Please proceed, Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, can you explain how you know about Bozovic's reporting line.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, I had opportunity to see him on both sides of the border in Bosnia and in Krajina. And I have seen him, well, not very often, but I'd say maybe two, three times a month at the headquarters of the 21st Corps. And he is a remarkable person when you see him. That would be the only officer I have ever seen to carry a sawn-off shotgun at the waist.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, to return to the matter of Arkan, what is your direct knowledge, if any, of Arkan and his involvement in the Pauk Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: To my knowledge, Arkan was just supplying the additional -- additional soldiers or additional fighters to the Pauk Command. Arkan wasn't there himself personally, but he had his people on the ground. And if I know Arkan from his previous involvements, it's got to be the money, otherwise he wouldn't be there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Do you know anything about Arkan's role in RSK before Pauk?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I only met him once, personally, and it was the meeting in hotel Topusko probably very early in 1992, just prior to arrival of UN forces. There were meetings of high-ranking officer of the JNA in the hotel. And they were trying to figure out what is the best way and fastest way to somehow normalise the life in the area. And Zeljko Raznjatovic busted in on this meeting and really abused the hell out of these people there. They were all generals who were very close to retirement. You know, they were not really, you know, a fighting unit, if you like. But -- and you can see on their faces they are really afraid of him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Do you know who Arkan was answerable to?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: To my knowledge, to the DB of Serbia, even before the conflict. Are we talking about the same man that the half of the Interpol in Europe was looking for? And he had a safe-haven in former Yugoslavia protected by the state security? The man is a known criminal, gangster. He was charged with bank robberies, he was charged with attempted murders, charged with escaping from prisons in Europe. That is not my kind of hero, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: On page 1 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus, could we ask the witness to clearly distinguish between who Arkan was answerable to, where his answer was primarily focussing on by whom he was protected. Even if I'm protected by someone, it doesn't necessarily mean that I'm answerable to that same person. Could you make that distinction and also explain to us what the basis of your knowledge is for -- for being answerable to, rather than being protected by.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour, I will give you a little known fact that I haven't mentioned this in this Court before. But there was an incident when Arkan was transporting weapon. And in the area of Bosnia, in a car. Him and a couple of his boys had a trunk full of weapons. They were stopped by police, searched, and arrested. This is just about the beginning of the conflict in Croatia. He was taken to Zagreb. And very shortly after, the people from Serbia state security and people from Croatia state security decided they were going to release him and not charge him. So he was working at the time both sides of the borders, for Serbian DB and the Croatian DB.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you give us a time-frame for this incident.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: October 1991. But that is a wild guess now, really.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's refrain --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... it was in the newspaper, it was on TV. So it is not something that I've discovered or come up by chance or ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: On page 12359 of your Milosevic testimony, you describe a meeting you were going to attend with the RSK minister of defence in UN Sector East. And you describe a chance meeting between a man named Stojkovic [phoen], aka Badza, and Arkan. Do you recall this event?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I was a part of the team that went to Sector East with Admiral Rakic who was appointed the minister of defence for RSK, even though we didn't have the navy. I always finds that amusing. Admiral Rakic. Anyway, as we were driving through Sector East --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry to leap up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I can see the interpreters throwing up a hand in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I fully can imagine that they do -- Again, Mr. Lazarevic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Guilty as charged. Okay. I will try to slow down. As I said, we were going to Sector East with the Admiral Rakic who was the minister of defence of the RSK, and I was in the car with him. There was a driver, Minister Rakic, and myself. The reason I happened to be there was purely for make it possible for Admiral Rakic to speak to the sector commander of Sector East.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And as we were driving through, passing by the petrol station which incorporated, like, a little restaurant with it, Rakic said, No, stop the car, stop the car. There's Arkan over there. So we stopped the car. I didn't get out of the car. He went in and he hugged Arkan and he hugged another man with him. And I was told by Minister Rakic that that was Badza, which I had no idea who he is. Later on, when I asked, they told me he is one high-ranking police officer from Serbia there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, what is your familiarity with Captain Dragan?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Captain Dragan, I haven't met personally, ever. All I know is what I heard about him. There was this myth going around that he was a superior in everything he does. So he was engaged to train the special police of RSK, and they would be wearing red berets so they can be recognised. He was, at the time, in the Sector South. And then, within a year, he just kind of dissolved in the air. And the last time I saw him was during the Saint Vitus Parade in Slunj, which is about like a three and a half years later. Though did I read about him, I have to admit.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court what your knowledge is of a man named Mile Novakovic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Mile Novakovic is a JNA colonel who became in a very short period of time a two-star general. So from lieutenant-colonel to two-star general, he made a very quick progress through there. And he was in command of Pauk, officially.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, you just mentioned the Saint Vitus Day parade in Slunj, so were you present during that celebration of the 28th of June, 1995?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have been there, during the parade.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, I'm going ask our Case Manager to play a clip from the recording, the video-tape of that celebration of Saint Vitus Day. The clip is from 65 ter 267, which is a segment from the full video. The full video being 65 ter 597, which is a related exhibit from the Milosevic case. Now the clip in 627 is from 29 seconds to the end. And that is -- corresponds to 1 hour, 32 minutes, 35 seconds; to 1 hour, 34 minutes from 65 ter 597.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus, I'll just briefly jump in here because Madam Registrar has assigned numbers to your list of documents. And in order to avoid that we are talking about 65 ter numbers rather than to -- about exhibit numbers ... Madam Registrar, could you tell us, we have a list of 24 associated exhibits. The numbers for those associates exhibits would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The numbers would be Exhibit P225 through Exhibit P248. And the 65 ter the counsel is referring to is not in the 92 ter package, I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
