utterances.text: I think she said it was, but I may have misunderstood her.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: 65 -- the 65 ter 627 is a segment of the 65 ter 597, which is in the -- in the exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. 597 would -- in this system, would be 2 -- P238. It's an excerpt from -- if I did not make any mistake ... Yes, as far as I can see the sequence on the list, it is part of P238, video of Saint Vitus Day celebration on 28th June, 1995. Let's look at the video.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Lazarevic, as we watch the video, please explain to us what you can tell us about what is taking place. And then afterwards I will show you two stills taken from this video and ask to you identify those whom you can recognise in those stills.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The day that I attended was the big parade to celebrate the Saint Vitus Day which was also the day that the battle of Kosovo was waged some 500 years ago. And it's a very special moment in the Serbian history which kind of beats me why would you celebrate your worse defeat ever? But something to do with the mentality, I guess. Now, the [indiscernible] was set up that in the middle within the military components of the parade and to the left where the guests of -- excuse me, the guests of the command and to the left were actually the international -- members of the international community, some military observers, officers from the UN Sector North, which I was leading because they were called in as guests.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One ...

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Could you explain to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One -- one second.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Sorry, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We've -- we have now looked at this video. There was text under it, apparently transcribing what was said. Since the witness was speaking at the same time, this text, I understand, is of no significance for this piece of evidence, or would it have any significance?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: If I understand correctly, Your Honour, the text is a narration from a video, the recording, so it was more important to us, Your Honours, what the witness would say about it, than the text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I see it is of more importance. But since it appears, I think it should be clear for reasons of transparency that we have not listened, neither was the text translated to us, so, therefore, what is in evidence is the video without the textual part of it, and so the pictures, the footage, as we saw it, and what the witness told us about it. That's what is in evidence. And if I say "it is in evidence," I was anticipating on the decision of the Chamber, that is, that P225 up to and including P248 are admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, can you explain to us, Mr. Lazarevic, what we saw as we watched that video-clip?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: What we saw? The beginning of the parade. Which happened [B/C/S spoken] or Saint Vitus Day, which was organised in the area of Slunj, basically was a PR stuff. You got a lot of guests, lot of officers from different countries, and we are going to show you how strong we are. The weapons shown there from the lunar rockets was borrowed from a neighbouring Republika Srpska and it was returned to them the following day. Nobody even tried to hide it. But you could notice on the trucks that were going in the parade that some them would carry the number plates from our own corps, and some of them wouldn't have any number plates whatsoever, making sure that nobody really can trace them. Which, since we allowed the TV crews to be there, we wanted actually everybody to see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. -- Mr. -- Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm now and then, apart from transcribers, interpreters also have great difficulties in following your speed of speech. Please proceed, slowly.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. With your leave, Your Honour, in light of the Chamber's comment and the witness's comment, with your leave we could replay that without the witness's commentary. I think the questioning will be more fluid thereafter. With your leave, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And would you like to us pay attention to the text as well?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I that I would be of assistance, yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we'll replay the video, and we'll receive the text transcribed and translated to us. And Mr. Lazarevic, therefore you are supposed not to say a word about it at this moment. Take a breath. Let's, again, listen to the video and look at the video. Have you provided the transcript to the booth?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "This is how the ceremonial Vidovdan parade of troops, which had been prepared for several days, was over in the best way possible. We had the opportunity to see our mainstays, the mainstays of our children's serene sleep, the mainstays of our future and our perspective. We had the opportunity to see that we have something more to hope for, even more than we had so far. We also have a modernly equipped, well-trained unit, which is composed of hardened and experienced soldiers. And all those who are here today at Slunj, and all of our honoured spectators who had the opportunity to follow our direct TV coverage from the Slunj parade ground, I'm convinced that you will ..."

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, we saw a line-up and an introduction of individuals. Can you describe, in that particular clip, what we were looking at?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Are we going to see the clip again, or you just want me to tell what happened? Well, in the clip itself, actually, you see just prior to the beginning of parade, you have president at the time Mr. Milan Martic being introduced by General Mrksic and by General Novakovic, the people in front of him on the parade ground there. If you look at it again, you could see General Mrksic, President Martic, and General Novakovic getting introduced to the people of the Pauk Command. First, on the left, would be Colonel Bozovic. Next to him was Colonel Ulemek, Legija, and there's a number of officers from western Bosnia that I'm not familiar with.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Could I ask the Court Officer, please, to call up a still from this video, which is 65 ter 3223, which is taken from the 48-second mark of that particular clip. And if the Court Usher could provide Mr. Lazarevic with a pen to mark the clip, the still, that would be helpful. I'm sorry, I'm advised it's 5223, not 3223. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Right there in the middle, you can see President Martic. Shall I put Martic on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Before you mark --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. One second. I see on other screens what I'm supposed to see on my screen as well, but which is not on my screen. And there it is. Please proceed. Could you please repeat your question so the witness can answer it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes. Before the witness -- before I ask the witness a question, I wanted to seek your leave to tender this still into evidence unmarked so that other witnesses might also mark it separately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, a number for this still, still unmarked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P249, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it that there's no objection against it, because that wouldn't make much sense, as a matter of fact. P249 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Lazarevic, could you tell us whom we see in this still, and we'll mark them one by one. You said, just before, you can see President Martic. Can you take your pen and write Martic, where you see Martic, please.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Right there in the middle. That is Martic with his hand extended. To the left on your screen you see the silhouette there, but in actual footage of the video, you can see this is a General Novakovic there. I put just G and N. Right there on the top of Mr. Martic is General Mrksic. General Mrksic. The gentleman right there, this is --

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Just to interrupt you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: For the record, the General Novakovic has been marked with GN, for Novakovic; and General Mrksic has been marked General with GM for Mrksic. Continue, please, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To the right, this young gentleman here, that's Colonel Ulemek. So I'll just put Colonel U. Behind him, you can only see the part of the face, that would be Colonel Bozovic. I'll put Colonel B. Now, this gentleman here, I have no idea who he is. Down there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: For the record, when you said have you no idea who he is, you're talking about the gentleman to the far extreme right on the photo. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Right. The one with the mustache and the beret.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Could you please now sign your name on the bottom of the photo.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And with that, Your Honours, we would like to tender this marked photograph into evidence, with your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the number would be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P250 Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P250, no objections. Therefore, P250 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Could the Court Officer please call up 65 ter 53, which is a still taken from later on in this video which is now admitted as Exhibit P238.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Sir, can you confirm that that is your handwriting on this photo?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now I'm going to ask our Case Manager, Mr. Laugel, to play a clip from Exhibit P61 -- sorry, yes, Exhibit 61 - from minutes 43:15 to 43:51. And after we watch this very brief clip, Mr. Lazarevic, I will ask you to tell us if you recognise anyone in the clip.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any text on the clip, Ms. Marcus?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, I believe, there is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And are we supposed to hear the translation? Is that ...

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's look at and listen to the video.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "I'm proud to present you with ... I'm proud to present you with this award."

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, did you recognise anyone in that video-clip?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have. Mr. Stanisic giving an award to Captain Dragan, a civilian. I mean, he's dressed as a civilian, not in uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you just a few more clarifications and elaborations in relation to your prior evidence. On page 12350, you were asked whether you became aware that Mr. Jovica Stanisic was present in the RSK when you were there. In answer, you stated: "Yes, I think I had the opportunity to meet the gentleman on two or three rather informal occasions in Knin." You were then asked if you were aware that he was present in relation to a dispute between Mr. Babic and Mr. Martic, and you replied: "Yes, indeed. And I believe that particular meeting with Mr. Stanisic came from Belgrade carrying a specific message from Mr. Slobodan Milosevic to Mr. Babic." Can you explain how you became aware of that event?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: The first time I met Mr. Stanisic was during the -- or after the Assembly session of declaring the RSK. We had a joint dinner. So this is the first time I met him. Admittedly, I have seen him before, I knew about him, but I have never met him. There was a bit of a turmoil going on, on political scene in the RSK at the time. Belgrade or Milosevic, if you like, did not like the idea of Babic remaining a president of the RSK. Apparently Babic did not follow to the fullest the ideas of Mr. Milosevic how things should be run. Somehow he believed that Krajina is his, he can do whatever he wants, he is the president. So he had to be replaced. And he got replaced by Milan Martic, a police officer. And since he refused to step down, in the end, he was forced to step down. And Mr. Stanisic came to tell him that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Can you tell us who invited to you that event?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I think the minister of information of RSK with Colonel Kosta Novakovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: You were then asked, on page 12350, whether you were aware of other times that Mr. Stanisic was present in the Krajina from your conversations with other officers. To that question, you replied that Toso Pajic would tell you that Stanisic had been --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Thank you for slowing down.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: To that question, you replied that Toso Pajic would tell you that Stanisic had been there or was coming. Although you were not in the police and thus you were not present at those other meetings, you said: "I'm pretty certain that Mr. Stanisic did come reasonably frequently to Krajina." Can you elaborate on what you meant when you said that you were "pretty certain that Mr. Stanisic came reasonably frequently to Krajina"?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: My relationship with Mr. Toso Pajic was a very close one. We met at least five times a week. If not more, five times at least. And sometimes he would offer me information which I didn't even ask for. But that's how close we were. I don't know, he believed that I should know, maybe, even though I was a member of the police force. So if I would happen to be in his office and he would say that he has to take a call from Belgrade from Mr. Stanisic about something, and then I would ask him, Do you want me to leave the office? No, no, it's okay. Stay. And then he would address him as daddy -- which, kind of -- I find it rather unusual that your superior is called daddy. I don't know. Any way, those situations were quite a few in three half years. So if he wasn't on the ground, I'm pretty sure he had a constant contact with the people on the ground, whether it is Pauk Command or whether it is Toso Pajic in area of the 21st Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: In relation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One ...

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: In relation to Mr. Stanisic's presence on the ground in the RSK in your area of responsibility, you stated in your prior evidence on page 12351: "I know at the beginning those visits were more frequent. I think probably due to organisational problems than anything else. At a later stage, Mr. Stanisic had his deputies or his right hands, or whatever you want to call them, who were actually present on a daily basis within the RSK." Who were these deputies or right hands to whom you were referring who were present on a daily basis within the RSK?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Frenki Simatovic would be one and Rajo Bozovic would be the other. Rajo Bozovic is Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: With the -- with respect to the second accused, Frenki Simatovic, you referred in your prior evidence to the name Stamatovic or Simatovic alternatively. Is this in fact the same person or is it two different people?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, 90 per cent of population in -- in Krajina knew him as Frenki. But some of the people would pronounce his surname as Simatovic and some would say Stamatovic. But it is referring to the same person.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: When asked if you had personal knowledge of him, you stated, on page 12352: "He was actually in possession of our former HQ in Petrova Gora. That's when he formed his own HQ with the special forces of the police from Serbia." What did you mean when you said "his own HQ"?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I meant -- I meant Pauk.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And how did you know that he had formed his own HQ with the special forces of the police from Serbia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: You have to understand that if you live in an area of responsibility which is only about 70 kilometres long and 15 kilometres wide not many things can happen that are you not aware of, especially if you are in a position to be -- I'm sorry, it says 730 kilometres; it's 70 kilometres. I'm looking at the screen here. Not many things can happen that are you not aware of or you haven't been told by others. And yet we are talking, here, maybe about, I don't know, five square miles. So first, as the 21st Corps, we were told to move out, that the MUP Serbia is coming to take over that command post officially. Later on, we discovered that a part of the command is going across the border into Bosnia to complete the HQ of Pauk. So if you look at the map or -- you will see that HQ which is -- the HQ of Pauk ... HQ of Pauk in Bosnia is only about 200 metres inside Bosnia, and the rest of the Pauk Command is in Petrova Gora which is in Krajina, about let's say 700 metres away. So between two commands, there's only about 800 to 900 metres in two countries.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Was there a particular insignia worn by these special forces from Serbia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: They had a shoulder patch which depicted a drawn upside down sword with a Serbian flag on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to see that emblem with your own eyes?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Frequently.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Could the Court Officer please call up 65 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Could the Court Officer please call up 65 ter 49. I'm sorry, I'm waiting for it on my screen. Does everyone else, see it?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Can you identify what we see in this photo?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Actually, if you look at the side, you see it better than if you like directly at it. There is that drawn sword, you got those inverted SSS on the side of it, and on the top is the Serbian flag.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Is this the patch to which you previously referred as the emblem worn by the special forces from Serbia in RSK?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Marcus. Will it be the Stanisic Defence or the Simatovic Defence who will cross-examine the witness first?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The Stanisic Defence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, I would like to continue for another 12 minutes, approximately, until the break. Mr. Lazarevic, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Jordash. Mr. Jordash is counsel for Mr. Stanisic. Mr. Jordash is also making some pauses between questions and answers, as you will do as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will try to.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel use the microphone with the long stem, to the right of him? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You spoke earlier today about the special police force in Serbia getting into the area of the 21st Corps. They came into that area at the time, is this right, when the 21st Corps moved from Petrova Gora. Were those two events simultaneous?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't call it simultaneous. Most of the -- or some of the members of the MUP Serbia came earlier on.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Who came earlier on and how many of them --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Some of the members. To understand the situation, on the roads straight through the area of the 21st Corps, there were check-points, roads blocks. And at one stage, I can't pin-point the date, we were told they will be coming, the trucks with supplies and manpower, that we are not to stop as they come to the check-points.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So members of the MUP Serbia came and started manning check-points in preparation -- no.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: No, misunderstanding. We, as the RSK, had the check-points, some held by police. But to go to Petrova Gora from whatever direction you're coming in, you have to go through the check-points along the roads somewhere. And we were told there will be members of the MUP Serbia coming through and to let them go without stopping or checking what they carry.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So the members were coming through on the way to Petrova Gora; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, do you know, or do you not?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I wasn't present when the very first one showed up. I'm aware of them moving into the HQ on Petrova Gora, setting it up. I am aware the members of the MUP Serbia coming for supplies in Topusko where I was, because the store where would they come is about 50 yards away from me. So I recognised the uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So their presence was, as you saw it, or heard about it, in preparation for the takeover of the Petrova Gora site?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: More than likely, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And are we talking days or weeks or months before they actually moved into that site?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Between the times when we moved out and dislocated -- dislocated. Displaced the HQ of the 21st Corps, and the time they took over, I don't think it is more than a month, in total.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So approximately -- should we say approximately a month?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Before you moved from Petrova Gora, the special forces of the MUP of Serbia moved into the Krajina, Republika Srpska Krajina district?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let's try to sort this out. We moved out of the Petrova Gora compound which is the old military compound. We moved out into new HQ. MUP Serbia started moving in. The moment they started moving in, the whole area was off limits to us. I couldn't go there or military observers or anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: We're talking about a month from when the members of the MUP Serbia coming into the district?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And then slowly moving into Petrova Gora, and you, 21st Corps, moving out?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me see whether there is any confusion. One month. Is that one month after you moved out until they moved in; or did they move in and did you move out only a month later? Which of the two?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We moved out. Within the month, they were in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jordash, from your questions it seems that you had understood perhaps the previous answer in a different way than I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So the whole process from the first Serbian MUP members coming into the Republika Srpska Krajina to them occupying Petrova Gora, approximately a month or two months?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: A month.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: A month, thank you. And you, the 21st Corps, moved to Vojnjik; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Vojnic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Vojnic. I think you may have to correct me several times. My pronunciation is quite bad, but I'm getting there. So you moved to Vojnic and that was, am I correct, 1994?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: No, I believe it is in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Whenabouts in 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Let's speculate now. We moved -- we move from -- from -- above hotel Topusko, late 1992, moved to Petrova Gora ... let's say May 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could I suggest that it was more like 1994. Could that be right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: No. Unless we look at my previous statement, then we can both be corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, your previous statement in the Milosevic trial, page 12320, suggests - let me just turn it up, so I don't misquote it. Now, if I actually turn to 12319, where you state, at line 20: "A. We have moved that HQ to Petrova Gora, used to be a JNA installation, and then from Petrova Gora to vicinity of Vojnic was the third and last displacement of the HQ. "Q. Can you approximate for us when the headquarters was moved to Petrova Gora? "A. It would be earlier 1993. Over the page: "Q. And can you approximate for us when you moved to Vojnic? "A. It was in the same year, at a later stage, when the Serbian MUP moved into Petrova Gora." So were you trying to say that it was later in 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could it have been at the end of 1993/1994? I suggest that the Serbian MUP did move into Petrova Gora but in November of 1994.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: No, absolutely incorrect. But May of 1995, we're done. And they were much longer there than just the six months.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, I want to ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Would you like me to continue, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it depends. As I said before, we'll have a break soon, a couple of minutes from now. If you would find this a more suitable moment, then we will have the break now before you start a new area.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we have a break and we resume at quarter to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, you may proceed. And, Mr. Lazarevic, breaks between question and answer, and between answer and question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm sorry I'm going have to return to the subject before the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could I refer to your previous testimony page 12422, and line 4 where you state: "It was late 1993 when there was a sudden influx of these uniformed men, uniforms I had never encountered before. Talking to them in our own language, it was obvious they were not from the area. Also it was obvious they were not a paramilitary unit, as far as we're concerned, because they were given a free passageway and also they were given our old HQ in Petrova Gora." So, please, would you think again whether you're suggesting that it was May 1993 or late 1993.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: It was in 1993, I'm absolutely convinced.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could I also then ask for Exhibit 405, please, the Pauk diary, to --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: But, before that comes, could I ask you this: Am I correct that the Serbian MUP arrived at the same time as other groups which you say were involved in Pauk? Let me put that differently: When the Serbian MUP arrived, Pauk started almost immediately?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: We have to make one thing clear first. I belonged to the military personnel. The movement of police within the RSK was not my focus. It wasn't my interest. This is just my observation. So if I'm saying late 1993, I believe it's late 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Whether the other units belonging to the Pauk Command came at the same time, at a different times, then I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you this: You obviously noted, as you've said in your evidence, that the arrival of the Serbian MUP was a significant affair. Was their arrival -- did their arrival coincide with the beginning of the Pauk operations?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could I please have Exhibit 405 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your reference is to --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- a 65 ter number or?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, Milosevic -- yeah, the 65 ter number, Your Honour. This is the -- exactly this. This is the exhibit I wanted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Segment of Pauk diary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Meanwhile, it is P235.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, have you seen this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Have you seen this diary before, or this log-book?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And have you confirmed, as far as you're concerned, it was accurate?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: That is difficult for me to say. I saw it for the first time only a couple days ago. I haven't seen it before.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So you can't confirm the contents of it are accurate?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I read it. I find it amusing. There is a mention of me in there as well, so I thought, well ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Can you have a look at the first page, there, operations log-book number 1 and then the date --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask a question. We're talking about years. The one thing apparently is not translated is the year on the title page.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know who is responsible for this translation, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yeah, could the first page be raised a little.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You see, I read in the original 16th/11/1994, G. Whereas I see there: 16 November 1990, which leaves open 1993, 1994, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: If we can have the bottom of the left-hand screen, please, I think that might assist Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it certainly does -- I'm primarily focussing on accuracy in whatever I see on paper. And perhaps we could -- this first page could be ... could be corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'm not going to labour the point, Mr. Lazarevic. But if that front page of the diary doesn't trigger your memory that the Serbian MUP arrived in November of 1994, then I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I do not agree with you. And I tell you why: This is a front page of operational diary. Somebody was writing down what was happening from day to day. Might be accurate. It doesn't necessary mean that the front page is accurate. Secondly, that is when already the combat situation according to this diary has started. Now, I'm referring to late 1993 when the first MUP units started arriving, so this is where we disagree. This is a time of operation, the combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, I'm not going to labour the point, but did you make the point, didn't you, that the arrival of the Serbian MUP had --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Late 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: -- had occurred at around the same time as the Pauk operations had commenced? If you made that -- you accept you made that point? We can move on, if you don't want to accept it, it's okay.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I'm still -- I'm still absolutely convinced it happened in late 1993 that the MUP made it to the Petrova Gora compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And before that time, before the arrival of the Serbian MUP at Petrova Gora, you hadn't heard of them in the Republika Srpska Krajina as a group, had you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And am I correct that you are unable to assist the Court with the training of the special police of the RSK in Knin, that you don't really know much about that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Not really. I can't help you there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: All you know about that from what you heard at the time, what you saw at the time, was that Dragan, Captain Dragan was training special police --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I never said I saw him training the special police. I heard about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You heard about it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You heard he was training the special police on behalf of Martic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And it was called Martic's police.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Exactly. And some of those men who had been trained at Dragan's camp wore red berets; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: So I heard, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And answered to Martic. Is that what you heard?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, they were called Martic's police; it is natural to assume they are responsible to Martic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yeah. And you, at that time, had a good knowledge, would you say, of what was going on in the Republika Srpska Krajina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: No. I never claimed I had a good knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, I think you said that if events that were occurring in a 70 kilometres by 50 kilometres there were not many things that would happen that you wouldn't be aware of. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: All the population living in that area would be aware what is going on, including myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Exactly. And the news coming out of Knin and Golubic was that Martic is training a special force?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: More or less, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Called the Martic's police?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: On behalf of Babic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: On whose behalf, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. Now you yourself wore a red beret; didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: On occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Why was that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I thought I looked better.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Were you trying to associate yourself with Martic's police?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did Martic's police, wearing red berets, have a particular reputation at that time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let me ask you about a different subject. I just want to make sure I understand your bibliography, your work bibliography, correctly. In 1991 you joined the JNA?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Late 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Late 1991.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Probably December 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And in early 1992, you were a liaison officer to the 21st Corps?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Originally I was assistant liaison officer to General Mrksic of the 8th Operational Group in Samarice.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. And at that time you started -- and this is your evidence, I think, that you started at around that time working with various translators?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: That come much later.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: When did that happen?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: The UN was deployed on the ground. They started looking for local people to work for them. So I'd say probably May/June 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May/June 1992, you're employed by KOS to --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: No, I was deployed by KOS in 1968.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, sir, if you would just let me finish.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You were employed by KOS in May or June 1992 in order to take - let me put that differently - to covertly obtain information from the UN and various international organisations, and you did that through taking information from the various translators involved in the international mission?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: What was the date again?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May/June 1992, when you started --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But you said in there that I was engaged in KOS by that time to gather the information through the translators in local --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: -- workforce.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Were you not?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: That was much earlier than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: When did you start working as an interpreter, taking -- organising other translators, and using that work in order to obtain information on behalf of others [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... I never worked as interpreter. I was a liaison officer of the 21st Corps. I was assisting the situation on the ground. But, obviously, you couldn't be everywhere at the same time, so they needed to employ more people. And everyone did employ their own translators, obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. Let me try to be a bit more specific.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let me just move backwards a bit. Is it your evidence that Stanisic received his information in 1991 and 1992, 1993, from the Republika Srpska Krajina mainly through Toso Pajic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yeah, I believe it to be the case, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Were you aware of anyone else giving him information?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Milos Pajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Anyone else?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Not that I know of.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Toso Pajic, though, was his, according to you, main information source?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, he was my information source as much as we exchanged ideas and thoughts and what is going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's return to the issue of the translation and translators. When did you start organising translators to provide information through your work as a KOS agent?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, as soon as they started giving them the jobs on the ground. It was the question of getting those informations which they attend to across to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And how long did that job last?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: To the very end.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Date, please.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: 5th of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And is this correct: Your job involved organising and briefing translators who were heading to various international or national meetings with the UN and so on? Please, you describe the job to me.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: The idea was, is they are, within the sector of the 21st Corps, they're going have a bunch of these interpreters to work for them on a local level. We're not talking about the international conferences and stuff like that. I never had to deal with those people. I'm talk about the local populace there. If -- if either of the general wanted to have his own interpreter to take him to Bihac when he goes over there, I wanted to know, or, rather, we wanted do know what was discussed on that particular meeting. So that that was the idea of getting them together, talking about the local interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And this was your main work for KOS from --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: No, it was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What was your main work for KOS during this time-period?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: If I was given a task -- well, I'll give you an example: During one of the international meetings, my only reason being there is to observe General -- Admiral Rakic because he was security risk to us. And that was not my -- that I made up that. I was told that he has got two sons living in Croatia who were of military age and they would -- and he is a military risk to us. But that is, for example, one of the tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: How often did you arrange translators between 1992 to 1995 to provide information?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Every time there was any meeting that we had put some relevance do it, yes, I would ask for information.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: How often would that occur between 1992 and 1995? Was it a weekly, a monthly, a daily affair?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: No. It happened as it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, give us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Everyone is going to make a break. I take you back at page -- because I was a bit confused. You asked earlier, Mr. Jordash, what the main source of information for Mr. Stanisic was. You suggested to the witness that it was mainly Toso Pajic. He said that he believed that that was case. You ask about another source of information. He mentioned Milos Pajic. And then, in the follow-up of that question, the explanation was that it was a source apparently for this witness, not primarily for Mr. Stanisic. I was a bit confused about whether Milos Pajic, where the witness said - and part of it is lost in the transcript at this moment: As much as we exchanged ideas and thoughts of what was going on. So, apparently, the conversation moved from the source of information for Mr. Stanisic to your source of information. I'm a bit confused by that. I just wanted to let you know that. And since we had to intervene anyhow, I do it at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we just clarify that quickly, Mr. Lazarevic. Milos Pajic was not your main source of information. He was Mr. Stanisic's, according to you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: No. I never said that. Officially, Mr. Milos Pajic was the member of the SDB.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Go on.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Right. Toso Pajic I consider to be my personal friend, and along the line of him being a liaison officer for the police in the area of 21st Corps and I was a military liaison officer, that we should meet and exchange what is going on, on the ground. So I wouldn't even call him my personal source of information about anybody. I want to make clear I didn't go and --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, we get the point. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, one of your principal jobs was to organise the translators; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I would test them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Right. And one of the ways in which you obtained information was directly from the translators who obtained it from the various meetings they attended; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now could you explain exactly how it worked, how it worked that the information came to you, and how it was it was passed on from you.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: It's very simple. If I, for example, heard that the, I don't know, Red Cross of Krnjak [phoen] needed to be -- International Red Cross in the presence of the UN, and we would have an interpreter there to translate. When it is done, I would ask him to write a very brief information what was discussed, what was the point of the meeting. And it was begin to me. Now, if I would get through the day three or four different information about the meetings, then I would compile them and try to make some sort of an overview of the informations, make my own conclusions, or try to draw what is going on from what I have got. And then I would pass that along to Nikola Zimonja or anybody in that sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What did you pass on? The original report or your composite report?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I would give a composite. I would give -- it was original report. I mean, if the person attended a meeting in a capacity of translator, I would ask him, What did you discuss? Do you remember what the points of the meetings? And things like that. In the information I got, I could get it either in writing or being told to me. This is what we talked about. There is a Croatian family needs, requests --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, can I just try to -- I'm going to be limited with time, so if we can just focus on the question. Did you write a composite report from the reports that were given to you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Depending how important it was. And it was my decision how important it was or wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: If it wasn't important, what would happen? Would you send the original report from the translator?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yeah, I would never receive the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You would never [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: When you say "report," I have the idea somebody is handing me a minutes from the meeting written by hand. And this is it, this is your copy, do whatever you want with it. This is it not the case. It was done -- a report can be by mouth, a report can be written down. But it is not an original document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No. Did the translators give you a written report?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: From time to time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did the translators most of the time give you an oral report?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: From time to time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Was there any other way the translators gave you a report?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... no, there is only two possibilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Overlapping speakers.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since the subject matter is translators, I thought you would think about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think what the witness said is that -- no, let's try to get that evidence again, because overlapping speakers even cause great problems at a later stage. The question was whether there was any other way the translators gave you a report. Your answer was? Two possibilities only: oral or written?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Or written, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That apparently was it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: If the -- if you considered the information you'd received important, you would write your own report about that information; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And what would you do with that report?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: First I would try to get it to whatever connection I had with Colonel Zimonja. If he was on the ground, give it directly to him. If not, find out who is the next one going to Belgrade so he can take it with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And is that a process you followed from 1992 to 1995?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, sometimes I was called in Belgrade to give a report in person.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: To who?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Colonel Zimonja.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did you give anyone else a report?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I think I worked one -- one task for -- now I'll give you the name; I'm not sure whether it is a real name or not. He was introduced to me as Medo, and he was a member of state security.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: We'll come do that in a minute.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So written report by you if information is it important enough, passed directly to Zimonja. That was the process.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So you cannot say, can you, what Zimonja did with that information?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I have no idea. For all I know, he picked it up and throw it in the trash. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So you cannot confirm or deny the suggestion that that information did not go to Mr. Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I never sent any report to Mr. Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And you don't know what Zimonja did with the reports?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And you never sent any report to Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And you never gave any reports to anyone other than Zimonja, did you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I did --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Expect -- sorry?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I gave to Toso Pajic. If I would -- if I would get a certain information, I'll give you an example: A battalion which was leaving the sector, an UN battalion, got in touch with me and said -- interested to sell all equipment they have, everything is, including those -- little listening devices, I don't know, part of weaponry, including even the mattresses for their beds, they were ready to sell everything. Now that information was given to Zimonja. Zimonja suggested I should get in touch with Pajic because the VJ was not interested in it. But, Zimonja -- Pajic might be interested in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So did you -- you gave the report to Pajic -- sorry. You gave the report to Pajic if Zimonja suggested that you do so.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: If he told me, yes, implicitly, You take this, you give it to Pajic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Otherwise, you just gave it to Zimonja?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yeah. Could I suggest you never had this role of passing information to Zimonja and, in fact, you were not a regular KOS agent.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: You can suggest whatever you want.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's now look at what your previous testimony was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let me read it to you, Mr. Witness. Referring to page -- to line 17 and the issue of the interpreters: "So I with have them go and come back and report to me about what was discussed at the meeting, what decisions were made, if any was made. And then I would compile all these reports in one major report which would -- was sent to my HQ. I would do those in triplicate, really, because one was going to Colonel Zimonja; one was going to the HQ, Colonel Bulat; and one was going do Toso Pajic." Isn't that quite different to what you just told the Court?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: No it isn't quite different.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: It isn't?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No. Okay. How is it not different?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: It is not different in that respect that I would give my report to Zimonja. If Zimonja suggested I should give a copy to Toso Pajic, I would give it to Toso Pajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: But in the Milosevic case you appeared to be saying that you did your report in triplicate, that each was going to Zimonja, Bulat, and Pajic, as a matter of course?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can I have a look at that, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Please could we have 12386 on the screen. I think it's P224.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The document is under seal. Would it be limited it to the -- if limited to the page and nothing else to be shown to the public, that is public on the Internet as well. So, therefore ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Have you read that, Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yeah. Line 20, 21, 22.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yeah. Any explanation? Or do you maintain that it is consistent with your account of earlier today?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, apparently it was different here.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: That's obvious. I either place it on not remembering, seing that the passage of time is 15 years. But I have an additional explanation for that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: There was -- there were situations where I was required to do a single report and only to Zimonja and nobody else. There were situations when I was told to do them in triplicate or in duplicate. But not on a regular basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let me ask you, please, to turn to --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Can we turn to the witness's first statement at -- made in 1999. I have forgotten whether this has been given a P number. I don't think it has. It is ERN 0205-3036.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, have you verified whether, on the basis of the limited portions of the testimony to be in private session, whether there is any reason for this statement to be kept confidential or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The statement I'm now trying to refer to, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, I think it should be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It should be confidential.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, I think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, therefore, it should then not been shown to the public. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Who told you, Mr. Witness, that you should do reports in triplicate or duplicate?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Zimonja.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Zimonja?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let me ask you to turn to the statement you made in 1999. You do recall making the statement? You've been through it on a number of occasions. I imagine --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I sincerely hope so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's turn directly to the eleventh page of the English version, and it is page 0205-3046 on the right-hand corner. In the B/C/S, perhaps I can be helped out by ... I'm looking for -- at the paragraph, Mr. Lazarevic, which begins with: "In early 1992, local and other Serbs interviewing for interpreters with the UN" and so on. I'm not sure what page it is. 10, in the B/C/S, thank you. 10. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And if you read that paragraph, and I'm interested in the second part of the paragraph where it says: "All of the interpreters were required to submit frequent reports back to me, and I forwarded these reports along with my own to Zimonja and Pajic." So "I forwarded these reports along with my own to Zimonja and Pajic." Isn't that -- did you find that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yeah, I'm looking at it. What about it?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, isn't that quite different to what you've told us?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Why is it different?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I'm telling you that I have been sending reports in accordance with the importance of the report --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Why are you suggesting there, in 1999, that you forwarded the reports of the interpreters along with your own report and you forwarded them on a routine basis to both Zimonja and Pajic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Only if Zimonja was insisting for me to send the report to Pajic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I waited a while to see where counsel was going with this. The witness has testified that he had two -- he had a dual role in the region. His testimony is that he had an official role within the 21st Corps and that he had a somewhat unofficial role with KOS. Which in -- which he says he had two lines of reporting. That's on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But let's not comment on the testimony of the witness. I mean, if you have any objection against the question --

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- that's fine. If you have the --

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, the objection --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What's the objection?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Sorry -- I'm sorry, Your Honour. The objection is that the question should be clear to witness which exactly role he is asking about in terms of reporting line. And that the two may be confused in the manner of questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Jordash, I leave it to you at this moment. In general, questions that confuse are not to -- put to a witness. At the same time, the fact that the Prosecution thinks that something may confuse the witness is not decisive of whether or not the question is confusing or not. I leave it into your hands so --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So know -- if you would be, yourself, convinced that it's mixing up matters, then you should refrain. But if you have good reasons to put it in the way you do it, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The whole paragraph -- just to be clear, the whole paragraph is quite clearly dealing with the KOS role, the whole paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you are putting your questions in that context?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And I can read the second sentence -- sorry, the sentence below what I have just read because this will bring the context: "The result was that every interpreter working with the UN and the ECMM in the Krajina was reporting back to the SDB and was on our payroll." That's what the statement says, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I would like to have a look at that one, too. Because I'm pretty sure never said that all -- what are you suggesting is the report from all over Krajina coming to me, and I'm just sending them forward?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, I'm just looking at your statement. I'm asking you about it. So would you have a look at that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yeah, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: It's same paragraph we just looked at. "All of these interpreters were required to submit frequent reports back to me, and I forwarded these reports along with my own to Zimonja and Pajic. The result was that every interpreter working with the UN and the ECMM in the Krajina was reporting back to the SDB and was on our payroll." Are you not -- in 1999, suggesting that all the interpreters were, by virtue of this surveillance scheme, let's call it that, reporting to Pajic and Pajic was reporting to the Serbian DB?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: On the area of the 21st Corps, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: But is --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Not all over Krajina. There's got to be some misunderstanding along the line somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, the misunderstanding is that in 1999 you said that you were reporting directly to Zimonja and Pajic; now you're saying that you're reporting only to Zimonja except when told by Zimonja to report do Pajic. And in the Milosevic trial you said something different again. That is the confusion I'm trying to get to.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, could you explain it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: What was the difference that I said during the trial in 2002?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, in the Milosevic trial, you said triplicate reports; in 1999 you said duplicate reports.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And now I'm saying nobody? What you're suggesting --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... trying to work out what you are saying now.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to try to be as clear as I possibly can. To understand the situation at the time, there were a lot of people involved in there from a different services; from a State Security Service, from the military intelligence, from a local police, and everybody else wanted to know what was going on. Now, my first response was to Colonel Zimonja. If, for example, you knew in advance where the meeting is going to be held and who is going to attend the meeting, then Zimonja might say, Well, this could be of interest to Pajic as well, so make a report to him. And I would do that. I don't see nothing strange.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: If that's your answer, we can move on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, actually, before we do move on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm slightly concerned about what is then shown to the witness. Do I -- the portion you were reading was apparently the top of page 11 in the English. And that was not -- the relevant portion apparently was not on the screen for the witness. And I'm always -- or am I wrong? In his own language?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I hoped it was because we did say page 10. So I'm not sure if --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did you, Mr. Lazarevic, see the section of the statement I was reading from?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Now you got me lost because we've seen so many things [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: let's try to be very precise on that. It can be that it is somewhere, but.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Perhaps it would have been better if I just refer to the English version since, Mr. Lazarevic ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, there are more people who want to follow the proceedings. So, therefore, it's -- of course, the witness is the most important one to be able to follow. But the others, like the accused, and those who are observing these proceedings. I just want always that we verify whether what we see in English is visible for the ... I haven't found it in the B/C/S version, but ...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: In the B/C/S version it is the central paragraph -- no, on the page that was shown earlier. Begin where the near 1992 appears. Except it's only the last portion of that paragraph that we see in English, on top of the English page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see it now. It's ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Page 10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it's in the middle of page 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Have you got that, Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, "In early 1992, the local and other ..." Is that the one that you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then later in this paragraph, close to the end well, let's say the last ten lines approximately, that's where you talk about the -- apparently about the interpreters being on the payroll. You found it? Where it says: "The result was that every interpreter working..." [B/C/S spoken] That's where you're supposed to read. You found it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, unfortunately, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Page 10 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those translators had our strict ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it's the line above that, I think, at least in the sentence before that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, in that case you have to go all the way up there and you see there was an agreement between Toso Pajic and Zimonja --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no, I'm just asking whether you found what was put to you as your statement which apparently is the the line starting with the result was that every interpreter ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, have I got it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's always be certain that if we put a statement or whatever to a witness, that he is able to read it and that everyone is able to follow what we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Sorry about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Have you read it, Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Any further comments to make?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, if you go back a few lines, you will find out there was an agreement between Mr. Pajic and Mr. Zimonja about the reporting line there, engaging the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, I don't follow your answer. Could you explain that a bit further, please?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let me just find the English version of it now. There's a line that goes: Those translators I have evaluated in Topusko in accordance with instructions from Pajic and Zimonja.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: So they were aware of each other trying to get the information. But Zimonja was -- who would be in advance decide who gets the information first.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Why would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And this is now found, apparently, on page 10 in the English, if I ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... in the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So you were suggesting in 1999 it was a joint operation between Zimonja and Pajic, a joint operation to work - let's put it like that - work the translators to obtain information for both of them?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't call it a joint operation. That's suggesting two of them decided it's going to be like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well you said --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: What I'm suggesting is that information which was interested to the police and there are information which are of interest to the military. They are not always one and the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, Mr. Lazarevic, you said in 1999, according to your statement: "I screened these translators into Topusko under instruction from Pajic and Zimonja, yes." So you were suggesting it was direct and joint operation, those two instructing you.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Now you are reading something that I never said.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So you didn't say that it was under instruction?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: No, no, I did say. But I'm not -- I have never mentioned that as a joint operation between the two of them. You have to realise that -- I was working basically two jobs there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, let me ask you a question.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did you say, as the paragraph states, they wanted to be in a position to control all of the interpreters?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I don't see any conflict there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did you say that? I'm just asking.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you say: I forwarded these reports, along with my own to Zimonja and Pajic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you say that as a consequence of that or the interpreters who were on the payroll of the SDB?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And now what you say is, in fact, I gave the reports to Zimonja, and Zimonja made a decision about whether he gave any of the reports to Pajic.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, if it is relevant to Mr. Pajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. Let's leave it at that. I think we might have exhausted the subject. Was there any other KOS agent that you gave information to in the years between 1991 and 1995?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Who?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember the names anymore, but there would be people coming in uniform, JNA uniform, from Belgrade asking for me and telling me Zimonja sent him. And I had no reason to doubt.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did you ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did you see the same KOS agents more than once, when Zimonja wasn't there to receive the reports?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Not that I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So you always got a new KOS agent picking up the reports when Zimonja wasn't around?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: More or less, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So, according to you, then, only Zimonja would be able to confirm your important work for KOS. Is that the sum total of what you're saying? Could anyone else?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: There were a lot of people who knew me there, what I'm doing, and how I'm doing, and everything else. I don't quite understand [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... would Toso Pajic know that you were a KOS agent?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: How would he not know, given that you were acting on his and Zimonja's behalf?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Because I was a liaison officer for the 21st Corps, and they both needed me at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If we continue this way, then I have to introduce a different regime, that is, I'll tell you you can now put a question; then I will give a sign that can you answer the question. But this is an impossible way of proceeding. Now, I give you a last chance to do it without my assistance as a traffic agent, or conductor, whatever you want to call it. Last chance.
