Otherwise, we really are going do split it up, because part of your testimony will be lost. Overlapping speakers just doesn't work.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: When I asked you, Mr. Witness, how would Pajic not know, you answered: "Because I was a liaison officer for the 21st Corps, and they both needed me at the time?" Could you explain that, please?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: At the time, police did not have their own liaison officer. Toso Pajic got given this task much later as a liaison officer for the police. So most of the time Toso Pajic relied on me to let him know what is going on, in relations to international community. So ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: But is this what you're suggesting to the Court, that, despite being instructed by Pajic to take information from the interpreters, despite seeing Pajic, I think you said five times a week, despite being in the office when Pajic speaks to Stanisic, Pajic would not know you were working for KOS?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: No I didn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no, one ... If you look at me, I'll give you a sign. Please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: No. There was no need what he should know. Officially, I was -- I was a liaison officer for the 21st Corps. My work concentrated on the war for KOS, and this is something you don't go around advertising. Toso, you know, I'm working for KOS and for you at the same time. This is simply not done.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What about Colonel Kosta Novakovic? Would he know? Wasn't he also working for the KOS internal security?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: He worked for external [sic] security.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I know. That's what you're saying --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whoa ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: But Novakovic worked for internal security, yes?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: That was my understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And Novakovic was Zimonja's superior?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Not that I knew of. That is news to me. If you claim that Kosta Novakovic was a superior to Zimonja, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So despite Novakovic working for the KOS, he wouldn't know about you either?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: No. I was not part of the internal security. You have to make a difference there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, Colonel Milos --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: My life I have spent outside of Yugoslavia working. So people on the ground in Yugoslavia, when I showed up eventually, had no clue who I am except those who I work with.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Colonel -- you've given this diagram which we looked at earlier, which I think is Exhibit 653, and you also named Colonel Petar Surla as working for KOS. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And Colonel Mlado Karan?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Mlado Karan. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: How was it that you knew about them working for KOS if they didn't know about you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I don't -- I don't get your question, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Why they didn't know what I do and I knew what they do? Because they were in position within the corps in a position of the -- of the internal security for the military. That was their corps. [B/C/S spoken].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Security officer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So the sum total then, is this a fair summary that no one can confirm, other than you, that you worked for KOS?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Probably some people who are aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could you consist the Court so that we might then, from the Defence, investigate?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. People who dealt with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Can you give us some names to assist our investigation?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: No, I can't remember any.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Can't remember any?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Really, why don't you get in touch with Colonel Zimonja and ask him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So from 1968 until 1995 the only name you can give who might assist is Zimonja?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay, fair enough. Let me ask you this about Mr. Pajic. You said today, earlier - and I will try to quote you - at page 27 of the draft transcript: "As I have stated before, I had at least five times a week meetings with Mr. Pajic because," something, "our work between the military and police, as far as UN forces on the ground are concerned. So quite frequently I would be in his office and I -- and he would tell me like, you know," something, "will be here. And I was led to believe that Daddy is Mr. Stanisic. He never actually, I have to be honest, he never said directly, I am working for Stanisic. But he did do all the work. It has been proven that he actually did work for Stanisic in the end." Right? So Pajic never confirmed to you that he worked for Stanisic. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Not in as many words.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So in the -- well, how long were you working with Pajic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Early 1991 -- I mean, late 1991 to 1995, the last person getting out of Krajina at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So not once during that period did Pajic say to you he worked for Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No. And your confirmation of -- sorry, let me put that differently. What you said to the Court earlier today was that it was proven that he actually did work for Stanisic because he ended up with an office in the DB headquarters in Belgrade, after 1995. Is that a fair summary?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And that's your evidence, that he worked for Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Now?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What's your evidence?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, my evidence is that what is happening on the ground, who was reporting to, who was he talking to, who was he being visited by, who we went -- who he went to see in Belgrade at the time, several occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, at some point, he was a minister of the interior.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: That's very late.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yeah. But he was, according to you, a member of the -- he was the chief the police in -- in Vojnic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Right. So you don't know what was discussed, if and when he went to Belgrade to see Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And what did he discuss when you were present during telephone calls to Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I wasn't really sitting there and spying on Mr. Toso Pajic. It would just happen that he would have a telephone call.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And he would have very brief answers on the phone. So I don't know what the other side is saying to him. If the first side says, Yes, yes, I understand, thank you, see you, bye, that's about it, that I can convey to you from the content of conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So basically you cannot confirm the contents of the conversation between Stanisic and Pajic, even though you were present?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: No, you can only hear one side of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Can you recall any of that conversation from the one side? Sorry.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: No, I can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. You mentioned earlier today, I think after the last break, that, on one occasion - is this right - you took a tape to someone called Medo who, you say, worked for the DB?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Other way around. I was given a tape by Medo and returned it to him after the meeting was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could you explain a little more? Where did you meet Medo, and what was the tape he gave you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: In the office of the DB, in Belgrade. I was given a folder consisting of a tape which would be initiated by the sound, start working. To take it to -- I believe it was Vukovar to a meeting with the former German ambassador and to record the full conversation that I had with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So you attended the DB office in Belgrade and was given a blank tape?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I was given the whole unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The tape recorder?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yeah. Which was built into a folder.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And the instruction was to take that to Vukovar to record the --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: To a meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: To record the former German ambassador? In a meeting.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And what did you -- did you do that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What did you do with the tape afterwards?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Brought it back to this person called Medo.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And who instructed you to go to pick up the tape from Medo in the first instance?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Zimonja.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And how do you know that Medo worked for the DB?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: That's what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What did he say then? Can you recall the words?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yeah, I don't remember the words. But I was led to believe that he represents the Sluzba Drzavne Bezbednosti, state security.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What was recorded from the German ambassador? What was contents of the tape?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I'm trying to think of it. I think the original, the whole idea was to get in touch with him and talk about his liaison with the journalist from "Duga" newspaper in Belgrade. That it was apparently his girlfriend or something like that, to get as much as I can out of this discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did you ever do that again for Medo?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Or the state security?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Not that I'm aware of. Now you got me doubting myself that Medo was from the state security. I believe he was. I was taken to a building which everybody knew was a state security building. With somebody from military going in there, how the hell do I know?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did you ever do it again for the state security?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Not that I was aware of, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could I ask you please to turn to your --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Can we have on the screen, please, the witness's 1999 statement, page 13 of the English version, and it's paragraph 4 of page 13. I'm going need to some help with getting the B/C/S. It's the -- sorry, it's not the diagram. It's the statement, which is P -- sorry, it's not P anything. It's -- that's the one. Now I want to have the B/C/S version too so that the witness can follow it clearly. It's the paragraph beginning: "I was being paid by both the RSK police/military and by KOS."

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I got the passage there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Right. There's a number of things which arise from this passage, Mr. Lazarevic. First, the first three sentences, or two sentences, three sentences: "I was being paid by both the RSK police/military and by KOS. I was required to submit my reports to Petar Surla throughout 1992 and 1993. In 1993, he was replaced by Mlado Karan, who remained in charge of KOS in Sector North until August 1995." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yeah, I'm reading, sir, but I have no idea what is happening here. Petar Surla left in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, if -- did you -- this contradicts what you said earlier, didn't it, about Surla and Karan not knowing that you worked for KOS?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: No, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So you didn't say this to the Prosecution in 1999?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I'm looking at it. I don't remember saying it. In all honesty. Looking at it, why would I say in 1999 that Surla was there in 1993 and in 1993 was replaced by Mlado Karan, which is totally incorrect?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, if that's -- if you cannot explain, then, how it got into your statement or why it hasn't been corrected in the very many interviews you've had with the Prosecution since --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Nobody ever paid any attention to it. I haven't.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: We're talking about 40-odd pages of very important material.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Let move on, Mr. Witness: "Surla and Karan sent all of my reports to Zimonja in Belgrade, and the tapes that I made of meetings were forwarded to a subordinate of Stanisic, who I knew only as Medo. He would take the tapes directly to Belgrade."

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: -- surprise to you as much as it is a surprise to me. I do not remember making this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I'm looking at that time. There are so many inconsistencies in that that I remember. First be, Mlado Karan and Petar Surla didn't work together. They replaced each other in the 21st Corps. Secondly, I never gave them anything to carry for me in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. If that's your -- you didn't say that to the Prosecution then?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: No. You can squeeze my thumbs, but I don't remember saying it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. Fair enough. Let's move on. And the point, then, about "tapes of meetings being forwarded to a subordinate of Stanisic, who I knew only as Medo," do you know how that got into your statement?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I remember one tape that I did for this person called Medo. I don't remember a multitude of tapes been sent.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you know how it got into your statement?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And then: "He would take the tapes directly to Belgrade." To -- from what you've told us, you went to Belgrade to give the one tape to Medo?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is it not happened in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: This particular case happen after the Krajina has fallen. I was in Belgrade by then, when I was asked to do this German ambassador.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: "It was Surla and Karan's decision what they would send to Knin." Do you know how that got into your report --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, I'm looking at the clock. We're close to where we have to conclude for the day. Could I inquire with you how much more time you would need?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I would like an hour, if that's possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How much time would the Simatovic Defence need, as matters stand now?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, at least two hours. We have a large number of documents that we would like to present to this witness, so we will not just chat here. We will have specific documents to confront this witness with. So we need at least two hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, I've already three hours on the list of wishes. What does that mean for the next witness to be called?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, by our calculation, we're not going to get to that witness so that we haven't brought that witness to The Hague, but they are readily available, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, it's -- my concern was the other way around, as a matter of fact, that the witness would be here. Under those circumstances, I think we -- we should endeavour to conclude the testimony of this witness tomorrow. Three hours is a little bit over two sessions. Let's -- let's try to -- to be as efficient as possible and to see where we come. Mr. Lazarevic, before we adjourn, I would like to instruct you that you should not speak to anyone or communicate in any other way with anyone about your testimony, whether that is what you have told us today, or what you'll tell us tomorrow. Refrain from any communication or conversation on your testimony. We adjourn, and we'll resume tomorrow, the 9th of February, quarter past 2.00 in this same courtroom, II.
